h1: Fishy or briny smells in beer and the rare causes behind them
title: Fishy or Briny Smells in Beer | Craft Beer School
desc: Why a beer can smell fishy or briny, the rare causes behind it from salty water to tired finings and how to tell a style choice from a fault.
teaser: Fish has no business in your pint. When it turns up, the cause is usually rare and often outside the brewery.
standfirst: A fishy or briny smell is one of the least common notes you will meet in beer. Sometimes it is the brewer's intention. More often it is a handling problem, a glass problem or water that carries too much salt.
sections: Fishy and briny are two different notes

Tasters lump these together, but they point to different places. Briny is a salty, sea-air impression. You feel it on the tongue as much as you smell it. Fishy is an aroma: the smell of a fish market, old prawns or low tide. Chemically, the classic fishy smell comes from amines, with trimethylamine the best known. Salt has no smell at all, so a briny note is mostly taste and suggestion.

Split them before you go looking for a cause. Ask whether the note is on the nose with your mouth closed or only once the beer hits your tongue. That one question halves the list of suspects.
When briny is the point of the beer

Some beers are meant to taste of the sea. Gose is a German wheat beer brewed with salt and coriander. A good one has a light salinity that makes you reach for the next sip. Oyster stouts are brewed with oysters or oyster shells in the boil. Several modern sour beers add sea salt on purpose.

In those beers a gentle briny edge is correct. It becomes a fault only when the salt is so strong that the beer tastes like a gargle, or when a fishy smell rides along with it. A gose should taste lightly salted, not like sea water. Read the label first. Our guide to reading a beer label covers the clues that tell you what the brewer intended.
Salty water the brewer did not mean to use

The most common accidental cause of a briny note is sodium in the brewing water. Most brewing water guides suggest keeping sodium under about 150 mg/L. Many brewers aim well below 100 mg/L. Above that, beer can taste harsh and salty, especially when sulphate is also high.

In India this is a real risk. Borewell water in coastal and dry inland areas can carry a lot of dissolved salt. The reading changes with the season and the water table. Water softeners that swap calcium for sodium make it worse. A brewery that never tests its incoming water can drift into salty beer without changing the recipe at all.
The rare causes of a fishy smell

A true fishy aroma is rare in packaged beer. When it does appear, these are the usual suspects:

  • Old or badly stored isinglass. Isinglass finings are made from fish swim bladders. Prepared properly and kept cold, they leave no smell. A finings solution left warm for days can spoil. That smell can carry into the beer.
  • Bacterial spoilage. Some spoilage organisms produce amines. A fishy note alongside sourness, haze or a ropy texture points to infection, not a recipe issue.
  • Taint from outside. Glasses washed in the same sink as kitchen pans or dried on a cloth that wiped a seafood counter can pick up a fishy smell. So can beer stored next to strong food in a cold room.

Rule out the glass before blaming the brewery. Pour the same beer into a clean glass rinsed only in fresh water and smell again.
Telling the causes apart at the table

You can narrow it down with three simple checks. First, a second glass: if the smell goes away, the problem was the glass or the bar. Second, a second can or bottle from a different batch: if it only shows in one, think spoilage or a bad finings dose. Third, the style: if the beer is a gose or an oyster stout and the note is briny rather than fishy, the brewer probably meant it.

A professional panel would go further and spike a neutral lager with a known amount of salt to find each taster's threshold. Thresholds for salt vary widely from one person to the next. That kind of calibration is hard to do alone, which is why trained panels work from shared reference samples rather than memory. Our guide to finding your own sensory thresholds shows how to start.
What to do next time you smell it

If you are a drinker, swap the glass and try again. If the note stays, tell the bar or the brewery politely with the batch code from the can. Brewers want this feedback. A rare fault is easier to trace when the report comes in fast.

If you brew, test your water before the next batch. A basic report giving sodium, chloride, sulphate, calcium and alkalinity costs far less than a tank of salty beer. Keep finings cold and use them within the time the supplier states.

Your first step is simple. Next time you open a gose, pour a plain lager beside it and taste them in turn. Learning what intended salinity tastes like is the fastest way to recognise the salt that nobody meant to put there.
faqs: Is a salty taste in beer always a fault?
No. Gose and some sour beers are brewed with salt on purpose. It becomes a fault when the salt is harsh or comes from brewing water nobody tested.
Can isinglass make beer taste of fish?
Properly prepared and stored isinglass leaves no fishy taste. Finings left warm for too long can spoil and carry an off smell into the beer.
Why does my beer smell fishy only in one bar?
That usually points to the glass or the glass washer. Glasses washed with kitchen pans or dried on a dirty cloth can pick up food smells.
